journal_name: IEEE Transactions on Intelligent Transportation Systems

abstracts.abstract: This paper presents a novel multi-layer graph neural network framework that fundamentally reimagines traffic flow modeling for heterogeneous transportation networks containing both autonomous and human-driven vehicles. Unlike conventional macroscopic or microscopic models that treat vehicle interactions through simplified assumptions, the proposed Dynamic Heterogeneous Graph Neural Network (DH-GNN) captures the complex spatiotemporal dependencies among heterogeneous road users through learnable edge dynamics and node-level attention mechanisms. The theoretical foundation rests on representing each traffic scenario as a heterogeneous graph where vehicles, infrastructure sensors, and road segments constitute distinct node types with heterogeneous relationship patterns. We derive rigorous mathematical conditions under which the proposed architecture achieves universal approximation of traffic flow dynamics, demonstrating that the learned representations are guaranteed to preserve essential traffic conservation laws. Extensive numerical experiments on synthetic and real-world traffic data from the NGSIM dataset validate that DH-GNN outperforms state-of-the-art baselines by 34.7% in prediction accuracy while reducing computational complexity from O(n²) to O(n log n) for large-scale networks. This work establishes a new paradigm for heterogeneous traffic modeling that integrates vehicle automation, transportation networks, and smart mobility concepts within a unified graph-theoretic framework, offering significant implications for intelligent transportation systems design.

This paper develops an enhanced stochastic traffic assignment model that significantly advances existing equilibrium models for urban transportation networks under mixed traffic conditions with connected autonomous vehicles. While traditional user equilibrium models assume deterministic travel times, the proposed Probabilistic Dual-Objective Stochastic Assignment (PDOSA) framework incorporates both travel time variability and communication reliability as decision factors for route choice. Building upon the seminal Dial's stochastic network loading algorithm, we introduce a novel logit-based path decomposition scheme that accounts for vehicle-to-infrastructure communication probabilities along alternative routes. The mathematical formulation establishes equivalence between the PDOSA model and a convex optimization problem, proving existence and uniqueness of equilibrium flows under mild assumptions. A tailored alternating direction method of multipliers algorithm enables efficient computation for large-scale networks with over 10,000 nodes. Numerical experiments on the Sioux Falls network and a real-world highway corridor demonstrate that PDOSA reduces average travel time prediction error by 23.4% compared to deterministic alternatives while providing statistically significant improvements in traffic control optimization. The proposed framework offers transportation management authorities a theoretically rigorous and computationally tractable tool for evaluating infrastructure investments and vehicular communications deployment strategies.

This paper introduces EdgeFlow, a groundbreaking edge computing architecture for real-time traffic control that fundamentally transforms the paradigm of centralized traffic management systems. Traditional approaches rely on cloud-based processing, introducing unacceptable latency for safety-critical decisions in autonomous vehicle environments. EdgeFlow distributes computational intelligence across a hierarchical fog-edge continuum, with roadside units performing millisecond-level local decisions while regional edge nodes handle coordinated multi-intersection optimization. The system architecture comprises three novel components: (1) a lightweight neural network inference engine optimized for resource-constrained edge devices achieving sub-5ms latency, (2) a distributed consensus protocol enabling autonomous negotiation among edge nodes without cloud dependency, and (3) a context-aware task migration mechanism that dynamically offloads complex optimization to higher-tier infrastructure. We implement EdgeFlow on commodity hardware using containerized microservices and validate through hardware-in-the-loop simulations with real intersection layouts from Singapore's expressway network. Experimental results demonstrate that EdgeFlow reduces traffic signal response time by 67% compared to cloud-based baselines while maintaining 99.97% system availability during network partitions. This paradigm-shifting architecture establishes a new design philosophy for intelligent infrastructure where real-time traffic prediction and adaptive control coexist at the network edge, enabling truly smart cities with autonomous mobility-on-demand services.

This paper presents TrafficComm 2.0, an enhanced vehicular communication system that substantially improves upon existing Dedicated Short-Range Communications (DSRC) and C-V2X standards for connected autonomous vehicle applications. The proposed system introduces three key architectural innovations: (1) an adaptive beamforming algorithm that dynamically adjusts antenna patterns based on real-time vehicle trajectory prediction, (2) a hybrid MAC protocol combining contention-based emergency messaging with scheduled access for regular cooperative awareness, and (3) a multi-hop topology control mechanism that optimizes relay selection through distributed reinforcement learning. TrafficComm 2.0 is implemented on software-defined radio platforms and evaluated through extensive field trials encompassing 50 vehicles navigating urban and highway scenarios. Results demonstrate significant improvements over IEEE 802.11p baselines: packet delivery ratio increases from 78% to 94% in dense traffic conditions, end-to-end latency decreases by 41% to 12ms, and network throughput improves by 58%. The system achieves reliable vehicle-to-everything communications at relative velocities up to 250 km/h, substantially expanding the operational envelope for highway automation. Deployment considerations for transportation networks include scalability analysis showing linear complexity growth and interoperability mechanisms enabling gradual migration from legacy infrastructure. TrafficComm 2.0 provides transportation authorities with a practical pathway toward full vehicular communications deployment supporting advanced traffic safety applications.
